# distil

> Context optimization for LLM agents, as an MCP server, a Rust crate and a
> measurement harness. It answers "where do this session's tokens actually go"
> and "does compressing this history pay for the prompt cache it invalidates",
> measured on real agent transcripts rather than on fixtures. MIT OR Apache-2.0.

distil counts a conversation by segment, prices a history rewrite against
prompt-cache multipliers, and exposes the result over MCP (JSON-RPC on stdio,
protocol 2024-11-05). It also ships composable layers that perform the
compression — but the point of the project is knowing when not to.

## The finding

Measured over 13,681 local Claude Code transcripts, 366,008 assistant turns,
195M tokens of unique text:

    tool results    117,460,908    60.1%
    tool calls       32,391,631    16.6%
    user text        29,363,474    15.0%
    assistant text   14,187,961     7.3%
    thinking          2,076,716     1.1%

Those 195M unique tokens were billed as 100.6 billion input tokens: every token
paid for 515 times, because a request resends the whole history.

Priced at real cache multipliers (read 0.1x, write 1.25x for the 5-minute TTL,
2.0x for the 1-hour):

    cache reads     97.8% of tokens    71.1% of cost
    cache writes     2.1% of tokens    28.1% of cost

Cache writes are 2% of the tokens and 28% of the bill. Editing history
invalidates the cached prefix from the edit onwards, converting reads at 0.1x
into writes at 1.25x or 2.0x. So a rewrite must shrink what it invalidates
below:

    turns remaining     5m TTL    1h TTL
     1                    8.0%      5.0%
    10                   46.5%     34.5%
    20                   63.5%     51.3%
   100                   89.7%     84.0%

That is the published break-even rule in another form: at every row,
cleared x turns / kept equals 11.5 for the 5-minute tier.

## What that means in practice

Layers that do not touch history are on the right side of the arithmetic:
CacheAlignLayer (orders content so the stable prefix stays cacheable) and
ScratchpadLayer (keeps working state outside the window).

Layers that rewrite history — MaskingLayer, SummarizationLayer,
CompactionLayer — cost more than they save in the common case. Reach for them
at one boundary only: context overflow, where the alternative is a failed
request and cache price stops being the comparison. BudgetLayer exists for
that moment.

For clearing old tool results, prefer the provider's own context editing:
it runs server-side, it takes clear_at_least, and it is one API parameter
against a dependency.

## MCP tools

    optimize     compress a conversation, reporting tokens before and after
                 plus a per-layer breakdown
    tool_call    handle the meta-tools distil injects (tool_search, note_read,
                 note_write)

## Install

    npx -y @munhq/distil

    claude mcp add distil -- npx -y @munhq/distil

No account, no API key, nothing to configure. The npm package is a wrapper that
fetches the release binary for the platform and verifies it against the
published checksums. install.sh and prebuilt binaries for six targets exist for
anyone without Node.

## Measuring your own corpus

    cargo build --features bench --release
    ./target/release/distil-bench ~/.claude/projects --json baseline.json

Reports where tokens are, what they cost, and the break-even table for your own
workload. The ratios above are one developer's machine; the absolute totals are
personal. Every source says to calibrate against your own traffic, and this is
the part nobody ships.

## Caveats

Counts use cl100k_base, which approximates Claude's tokenizer within a few
percent. The break-even model assumes a single cache breakpoint, so a rewrite
confined to the tail costs less than the table shows — that refines it, it does
not reverse it.
